games.explanation: Luzardo is a buzzsaw against lefties and roughly a league-average arm against everyone else, which matters because St. Louis is going to send a right-handed heavy lineup that neutralizes the half of his game that scares people. Herrera in particular is the kind of righty bat that turns Luzardo mortal, and Burleson and Walker aren't giving away at-bats against the fastball either. Dobbins is nobody's ace, but the projected margin here is less than half a run and the market has this priced like Philly is the clearly better team. At +190 on a coin flip disguised as a mismatch, the number is doing the work.

The market is pricing this like the Yankees are the clear favorite, but the projected score is a dead heat and the Elo gap is two points, which is to say no gap at all. Schlittler is a fine arm who happens to walk righties at a near-double-digit clip, and Toronto runs a lineup that punishes exactly that, with Springer sitting on a .415 xwOBA against right-handers and Kirk quietly hard-hitting everything in sight. Arrighetti is the shakier starter, sure, but a coin-flip game at plus money doesn't require your guy to win it, only for the other guy to be mortal. At +215, you're getting paid better than two-to-one on what our model sees as a game inside the margin of error.

The market keeps pricing the White Sox like they've earned the right to be a live dog, and they simply have not. Sean Burke walks the ballpark and gives up loud contact to righties, which is unfortunate news when Lindor and Bichette are the first two names on the card and posting north of a .350 xwOBA against right-handed pitching. Manaea is the steadier arm by a comfortable margin, and a Chicago lineup fronted by Meidroth and Vargas is not the group you want chasing a lead against a lefty missing bats at a 28% clip. Getting plus money on the better team, the better starter, and the better lineup is the entire pitch.

Yamamoto is a fine pitcher having a fine year, but plus-money underdog prices exist because coin flips get mispriced when the name on the marquee is loud enough. Pittsburgh sends three lefty-leaning bats to the top of the order against a righty who has been noticeably more hittable from that side, with Brandon Lowe in particular the kind of pull-happy barrel threat you do not want in a park playing this homer-friendly. Chandler is not Yamamoto, but he does not need to be for a game the simulation sees decided by less than half a run. At +200 you are getting a real team at a lottery-ticket number, and the ticket is closer to a coin flip than the board wants to admit.

The Dodgers are the better team, nobody's arguing that, but a run and a half is a lot of cushion to give a Pirates lineup that actually swings the bat against right-handed pitching. Yamamoto has been dominant overall, but his splits vs righties tell a quieter story, with a barrel rate against that jumps to 8.7% and a hard-hit rate closer to 49%, and Pittsburgh happens to run Lowe and Reynolds out there against exactly that profile. Bubba Chandler isn't going to overwhelm this Dodgers lineup, but he doesn't have to, he just has to keep it close, and a Chavez Ravine forecast with heavy HR park factors cuts both ways. At plus money on the runline, you're getting paid to bet that a projected one-run game stays a one-run game.
